column1: Lack of Backend Sanitization for Address/Location Parameter
column26: h3. 🐞 Bug Summary During security testing using *Burp Suite*, I identified that the backend server does not sanitize HTML/JavaScript payloads sent via the {{address}} parameter. While the Frontend currently mitigates the risk by auto-escaping characters, the Backend accepts and reflects raw tags in the JSON response. This poses a significant *Stored XSS* risk if this data is rendered in other un-sanitized areas of the platform (e.g., Admin Dashboards, Order History, or Email templates). ---- h3. 🔁 Steps to Reproduce * Open Burp Suite * Click on Proxy and make sure Intercept is OFF * Open Browser from Burp and go to WeGo Homepage: [https://wegodelivery.app/en|https://wegodelivery.app/en|smart-link] * Type any city in the "enter delivery address" parameter, but don't Hit Enter * In Burp turn ON Intercept * Return to the browser and hit enter * Return to Burp and click on the request that shows the city you entered * In the Inspector section change the value of your city with * Click Forward * Check the history section and the browser * Analyze the server response. ---- h3. ✅ Expected Result The server should sanitize the input by converting special characters to HTML entities (e.g., {{<}} becomes {{<}}) or reject the request if it contains forbidden tags. ---- h3. ❌ Actual Result The server reflects the raw, un-sanitized payload in the JSON response: {{"address":"-->"}} ---- h3. 🔥 Severity * High ---- h3. 🌍 Environment * OS: Windows 11 * Browser: Burp Chrome * Device: laptop Acer aspire lite 16 ---- h3. 📌 Impact Although the frontend currently mitigates the risk via auto-escaping, the *backend's failure to sanitize input* poses a high risk of *Stored or Blind XSS*. # *Administrative Compromise:* Malicious payloads stored in the database could be executed in the *Admin Dashboard* (which may have different security configurations), leading to *Session Hijacking* or *Account Takeover* of staff accounts. # *Lateral Movement:* The unsanitized data could propagate to internal systems (logs, support tickets, email templates) where it could be executed. # *Data Integrity:* Allows for *HTML Injection*, which can be used to deface parts of the application or conduct phishing attacks against other users. ---- h3. 📎 Attachments !image-20260312-110224.png|width=686,alt="image-20260312-110224.png"!

column1: [PERFORMANCE] Critical Load Time Discrepancy: Mobile LCP (6.5s) vs. Desktop (0.9s)
column26:
A performance audit using Google Lighthouse reveals a significant gap between the Desktop and Mobile experience. While the Desktop version achieves an elite performance score (*98*), the Mobile version is struggling at *50*, primarily due to a critically high *Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)*.

In a competitive delivery market, mobile users expect near-instant loading. Current metrics show that mobile users are waiting over 6 seconds before the main content is visible.

h3. *Business Impact*

* *User Retention:* 53% of mobile users abandon sites that take longer than 3 seconds to load. Our current 6.5s LCP puts us at high risk of losing customers to competitors.
* *SEO:* Google prioritizes Core Web Vitals (LCP, TBT) for mobile indexing. This performance gap may negatively affect our search engine ranking.

h3. *Steps to Reproduce* Open *Google Chrome* in *Incognito Mode* (to ensure no extensions interfere with performance).

# Navigate to the Wego Homepage: [WEGO24 Business|https://wegodelivery.app/en]
# Open *Chrome DevTools* ({{F12}} or {{Right Click -> Inspect}}).
# Go to the *Lighthouse* tab.
# Configure the following settings for the first run:
#* *Mode:* Navigation (Default)
#* *Device:* *Mobile*
#* *Categories:* Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO.
# Click *"Analyze page load"* and wait for the report.
# Repeat the process by switching the *Device* to *Desktop* for comparison.

h3. *Environment Details*

* *Device Type:* Laptop
* *Operating System:* Windows 11 *Browser:* EDGE - *Incognito Mode*
* *Network Connection:*  Stable Home Wi-Fi / 1GB
* *Lighthouse Throttling (Mobile):* Simulated Moto G Power, Slow 4G (Default Lighthouse Mobile profile)

----

h3. *Proposed Technical Solutions*

Based on the Lighthouse audit, we recommend the following optimizations:

# *Eliminate Render-Blocking Resources:* Currently causing a delay of ~1,090ms on mobile. Defer non-critical CSS/JS.
# *Optimize LCP Image:* Implement {{<link rel="preload">}} for the main hero image (e.g., the burger/delivery banner) to ensure it starts loading immediately.
# *Font Loading Strategy:* Use {{font-display: swap}} in CSS to ensure text remains visible while custom fonts are loading.
# *Image Compression:* Serve images in next-gen formats (WebP or AVIF) and ensure they are properly sized for mobile viewports.
# *Cache Policy:* Extend cache lifetimes for static assets to improve load times for returning users.

h3. Issue 1: Fake emails accepted

*Root cause:* The email validation only checked RFC format (Zod {{.email()}}), with no domain-level filtering. Any syntactically valid email like {{test@mailinator.com}} would pass and trigger a Supabase OTP magic link send.

*Fix:* Added a disposable email domain blocklist (~100 known providers) to the {{emailSchema}} in {{customer-auth-schemas.ts}}. The check:

* Runs after email normalization (trim + lowercase)
* Uses efficient Set lookup (O(1))
* Applies to both customer login and signup flows (shared schema)
* Shows error: "Temporary or disposable email addresses are not allowed"
* Blocks: mailinator.com, yopmail.com, guerrillamail.com, temp-mail.org, and ~96 more

*Tests:* 5 new test cases added, all passing (38 total).

h3. Issue 2: Real emails — verification sent but never received

This is a *Supabase SMTP delivery issue* outside our application code. Supabase Auth handles magic link email sending via their own SMTP infrastructure. Possible causes:

* Emails landing in spam folders
* Supabase email rate limits
* Email provider delivery delays

This should be investigated in the Supabase dashboard under Auth > Email Templates and Logs.

h3. Files Changed

* {{apps/web/src/lib/auth/disposable-email-domains.ts}} — new blocklist (100 domains)
* {{apps/web/src/lib/auth/customer-auth-schemas.ts}} — email schema with disposable check
* {{apps/web/src/lib/auth/customer-auth-schemas.test.ts}} — 5 new test cases

column1: 🔐 Security Bug – Stored XSS in Profile Name Field
column26: h3. 🐞 Bug Summary The Profile Name input field allows malicious code injection (Stored XSS). Input is not sanitized, validated, or escaped, allowing HTML/JS payloads to be saved and executed. ---- h3. 🔁 Steps to Reproduce # Log into the application. # Navigate to *Profile → Edit Profile*. # In the *Name* field, enter a malicious payload, for example: OR "> # Save changes. # Return to the profile page or any page where the name is displayed. ---- h3. ✅ Expected Result * The input should be sanitized. * HTML/JS code must NOT be stored or executed. * The name should remain plain text only. * Application should reject dangerous characters ({{<}}, {{>}}, {{"}}, {{'}}, {{/}}, etc.) ---- h3. ❌ Actual Result * The application *accepts* the malicious input. * The payload is *stored in the database*. * The injected code is *displayed unsanitized*. * JavaScript executes when the profile loads → *Stored XSS vulnerability*. ---- h3. 🔥 Severity * Critical ---- h3. 🌍 Environment * OS: Windows 11 * Browser: Edge * Device: Pc ---- h3. 📌 Impact * Compromises all users viewing the infected profile * Allows execution of arbitrary JavaScript * Can steal session tokens, cookies, and sensitive data * Violates OWASP Top 10 – A03 Injection ---- h3. 📎 Attachments !image-20260220-131751.png|width=671,alt="image-20260220-131751.png"!

24/Feb/26 12:09 PM;712020:b2a39849-1f84-43df-9964-f5586bb81e48;h2. Fix Deployed — {{63852ad}} on {{main}}

h3. Investigation

React's JSX auto-escaping already prevents XSS when rendering — {{dangerouslySetInnerHTML}} is not used anywhere in the codebase. A payload like {{<script>alert('XSS')</script>}} entered in the profile name field would display as literal text, not execute.

However, storing unsanitized HTML in the database is still a defense-in-depth concern (future code could introduce unsafe rendering patterns).

h3. Changes Made

# *Extracted* {{sanitizeTextInput()}} to {{@wego/utils}} — shared function that strips HTML tags ({{<[^>]*>}}), unclosed {{<}} characters, and control characters including DEL ({{\x7F}})
# *Applied* {{.transform(sanitizeTextInput).pipe(z.string().min(N))}} to all user-facing text fields:
#* Restaurant name, description
#* Menu category name, description
#* Menu item name, description
#* Modifier group name, description
#* Modifier name
#* Order notes, reject/cancel reasons
#* Special instructions (cart, checkout, order items, orders)
#* Delivery instructions
#* Restaurant and driver reviews
#* Profile fullName
# *Post-sanitization validation* — {{.pipe()}} re-validates min-length after HTML stripping, so a payload like {{<script>}} (8 chars, passes min(1)) gets stripped to {{""}} and correctly rejected

h3. Files Changed

* {{packages/utils/src/index.ts}} — new shared {{sanitizeTextInput}} export
* {{packages/utils/src/restaurant-schemas.ts}} — sanitization on all text fields
* {{packages/utils/src/customer-schemas.ts}} — sanitization on all text fields
* {{apps/web/src/app/api/profile/route.ts}} — uses shared import instead of local copy

column1: SECURITY BUG - Authentication Tokens Visible in document.cookie (Client-Side Exposure)
column26:
h3. 🐞 Bug Summary

When executing {{document.cookie}} in browser DevTools, authentication-related cookies and tokens are returned in plain text, including:

* Stripe session identifiers
* Locale settings
* *Auth tokens (*{{sb-…-auth-token}}*) for the logged-in user*
* Tokens containing:
** Base64-encoded JWT
** User personal information (name, email)
** Refresh tokens
** Expiration timestamps
** Authentication provider details

These values *should never be accessible in plaintext on the client side*, because they allow attackers to:

* Hijack user sessions
* Perform account takeover
* Impersonate authenticated users
* Bypass login mechanisms
* Steal sensitive personal data

This is a *major security vulnerability*.

----

h3. 🔁 Steps to Reproduce

# Log in to the application normally.
# Open browser *Developer Tools* → *Console*.
# Type the following: document.cookie
# Press Enter.
# Observe the returned cookie string which includes *authentication tokens and user data*.

----

h3. ✅ Expected Result

Authentication tokens *must NEVER be stored in accessible cookies*.

Correct security behavior:

* {{document.cookie}} should return *no auth-sensitive data*.
* Tokens should be stored *securely*, for example:
** HttpOnly cookies (not readable by JavaScript)
** Secure cookies (HTTPS only)
** SameSite=Lax or Strict
** Or server-side sessions

----

h3. ❌ Actual Result

{{document.cookie}} reveals multiple sensitive cookies, including:

* {{__stripe_mid}}
* {{NEXT_LOCALE}}
* {{sb-xxx-auth-token.0}}
* {{sb-xxx-auth-token.1}}

Contents include:

✔ Access token
✔ Refresh token
✔ JWT payload
✔ User full name
✔ Google auth provider details
✔ User email
✔ Token expiration
✔ Provider metadata

----

h3. 🔥 Severity

* Critical 

----

h3. 🌍 Environment

* OS: Windows 11
* Browser: Edge
* Device: Pc

----

h3. 📌 Impact

If an attacker can access the browser (even through XSS), they can:

* Steal authentication tokens
* Log in as the user
* Access personal data
* Perform privileged actions
* Persist long-term sessions using refresh tokens

This can lead to:

🔥 *Full Account Takeover*
🔥 *Data Exposure*
🔥 *Compliance Violations (GDPR)*
🔥 *Session Hijacking*

----

24/Feb/26 11:54 AM;712020:b2a39849-1f84-43df-9964-f5586bb81e48;h2. Investigation Result: By Design (Supabase SSR Architecture)

h3. Research Summary

After researching Supabase's official documentation and community discussions, this is *expected behavior* for Supabase Auth with SSR — not a vulnerability in our implementation.

*Supabase official docs (*[*How do I make the cookies HttpOnly?*|https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/how-do-i-make-the-cookies-httponly-vwweFx]*):*

{quote}"This is not necessary. Both the access token and refresh token are designed to be passed around to different components in your application. The browser-based side of your application needs access to the refresh token to properly maintain a browser session anyway."{quote}

*Supabase maintainer @hf (*[*GitHub Discussion #12303*|https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/12303]*):*

{quote}"HTTP-Only cookies are not an option unless you're making a very traditional web app."{quote}

h3. Why HttpOnly cookies would break our app

Setting cookies to {{httpOnly}} would disable:

* {{onAuthStateChange()}} — client can't detect login/logout
* Client-side {{getUser()}} — all React Query hooks break
* Supabase Realtime subscriptions (order tracking, driver location)
* All Zustand store auth flows

h3. Mitigations already in place

Our {{cookie-options.ts}} follows Supabase's recommended best practices:

||Defense||Status||
|{{secure: true}} (HTTPS-only in production)|Implemented|
|{{sameSite: 'lax'}} (CSRF protection)|Implemented|
|{{maxAge: 7 days}} (reduced from Supabase's 400-day default)|Implemented|
|Content Security Policy (CSP) with strict allowlists|Implemented|
|CSP violation reporting endpoint|Implemented|
|{{Strict-Transport-Security}} (HSTS with preload)|Implemented|
|{{X-Frame-Options: DENY}} (clickjacking prevention)|Implemented|
|{{X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff}}|Implemented|

h3. Conclusion

The attack scenario described ("if an attacker can access the browser through XSS") is mitigated by *preventing XSS in the first place*, which is handled by our CSP headers and addressed further in KAN-9 (Stored XSS fix). Making cookies HttpOnly is not feasible with Supabase's architecture and is explicitly not recommended by Supabase.
